Changelog

What changed in Rukoo Mail, in plain English.

Rukoo Mail is an email app for your computer and phone. You read and write mail in it, see your calendar next to your mail, and can chat with an AI assistant that you connect yourself. This page tells the story version by version, newest first, and shows what each change looks like.

3 November 20262.3.0

Meeting notes you can write in properly

Formatted meeting notes, tidier screen pictures, and meeting chats that start with the meeting.

Version 2.3.0 polished meetings. It was a focused release with one public code change and a full set of public screenshots.

Meeting notes now use the same formatting and link controls as the mail writer. You can make text bold, add lists and links, and the notes keep their formatting when you reopen them. Under the surface they save in a simple text form that other note apps can read. The notes area beside the meeting text got wider, so you can write without squeezing the text of the call out of sight. The Notes tab can also use the full width when you want room to write.

Screen pictures in the meeting text got tidier. Pictures that look almost the same, such as a slide that barely changes, now fold together into one compact row. Opening the row shows a strip with the other pictures. A Screen switch remembers whether you want to see screen pictures at all.

Chats inside a meeting now start with the meeting as their subject, not with whatever email happened to be open. The phone follows the same rule. Behind the scenes, a Hermes assistant now sees the combined tools of every device that answers, so an older phone that answers first can no longer hide the computer's meeting tools. Each request still goes to the device that owns the chat. If you use Hermes, this version needs one manual step: copy the new connecting file to the Hermes computer and tell your assistant to reload. Updating Rukoo alone does not update that file. The release notes link the setup guide for this step.

Saving notes got more careful. Typed lines, soft line breaks, formatted links and blank lines inside lists survive a save and a restart. If notes grow too large to save, Rukoo shows an error and keeps the last saved version intact instead of overwriting it with a broken one. Shorten unsaved notes before you close Rukoo in that rare case, because the unsaved text only lives until the app closes. The phone version that traveled with 2.3.0 was 0.5.1.

The release notes end with an honest testing note, and it is worth repeating here. The automatic meeting checks used a pretend Voice and test assistants that follow a script. A live Hermes connection with an older phone in the mix, and real Voice recording and live writing on a real call, had not been verified for this version when it shipped.

Release notes for 2.3.0 on GitHub

3 November 2026Voice 0.1.0

Speak instead of type

Rukoo Voice types what you say anywhere in Windows, and records meetings for Rukoo.

Rukoo Voice is a small Windows companion app. It does two jobs. It lets you dictate text anywhere in Windows. And it records your meetings for Rukoo. It replaces an older dictation app called Ownkey. Meetings need Rukoo 2.2.0. Voice has its own version numbers and its own downloads.

For dictation, you hold the right Alt key, speak, and let go. Voice types the text into the app you are in. If you select text first and hold the right Ctrl key, you can give a spoken instruction such as "make this shorter", and Voice rewrites the selected text. The words can be typed out on your own computer, with no internet needed, or by an online service with your own key. Rewriting offers the same choice between services on your computer and services online. A personal dictionary, fixed corrections for words it often hears wrong, removal of filler words such as "um", and automatic rewriting all came over from Ownkey. Voice restores your clipboard after it pastes, and it keeps dictated text out of your clipboard history. On its first start it imported Ownkey's settings and reused the speech files Ownkey had already downloaded. It never wrote into Ownkey's folders. The release notes add one practical warning: quit Ownkey before you start Voice, or give one of them other keys, because both listen to the same two keys.

For meetings, Voice records your microphone and the sound of the call in a separate recording program. That split is deliberate. If Voice or Rukoo crashes, the recording goes on. If the recorder itself stops, Voice restarts it into the same meeting and marks the gap. Voice writes down what is said while you talk, on your own computer unless you choose an online service, and sends the text to Rukoo as it goes. An online service only receives meeting sound after you agree to it for that service. You can start and stop a meeting from the pill, from the tray near the clock, or from Rukoo. By default, Voice keeps the sound for 7 days after it has been written down, then removes it. The text stays.

Voice told up to eight voices on the call apart while it recorded. Rukoo then turned "Speaker 2" into a name from the guests of the calendar appointment. The numbers kept their meaning when a part of Voice restarted, so Speaker 2 did not suddenly become someone else halfway through. By default this listening happened on your own computer, so the call sound stayed with you. It needed a fairly recent processor, and the settings said in normal words why the labels were off when they were off: the processor misses a needed ability, a speech file is missing, or you have not agreed to send sound online. If you chose an online live service for meetings and agreed to it, that service labeled the voices together with writing the text.

Each meeting could also record the screen: off, still pictures, or video. Voice settings held the normal choice, and Rukoo could choose per meeting. With still pictures, Voice saved a picture each time the screen changed in a clear way, plus the text it could read on that picture, on the same clock as the sound. With video, it saved a film made by your graphics card in small pieces, so a crash lost a second or two at most. Voice recorded one screen at a time, starting with the screen that held the call, and you could switch screens during the meeting. If the disk filled up or the film maker failed, Voice dropped the video first, then the pictures, and never the sound. The pill said what it had dropped. A meeting started from Voice waited up to half a second for Rukoo to hide its windows before screen recording began. Sound never waited.

Voice could back up each meeting to online storage that you rent yourself, such as UpCloud or Cloudflare storage. You had to pass a connection test before backup would turn on. Voice locked every file on your computer before upload, so the storage company could not listen. The key and the storage password were protected by Windows for your user account. You got a recovery code to open meetings on another computer. Without it, nobody can open them, including you. Sound and pictures uploaded during the meeting, video after it. An interrupted upload continued where it stopped. Voice kept any material that had not reached backup yet, as long as 10 gigabytes of disk stayed free. Assistants on another computer could reach meeting sound, a picture or a short film through Rukoo, with a link that worked for five minutes. The key itself never left Voice.

The limits of this first Voice version were listed plainly. Voice runs on Windows only. Its installer is not signed yet, so Windows warns before the first start and you choose "More info", then "Run anyway". The same warning applies to Rukoo itself. Video needs a graphics card that can make films. Without one, Voice records pictures only. On a busy laptop with four processor cores, speaker labels can fall behind the call. Voice records everything the computer plays, not the sound of one app alone. Its update check, if you turn it on, tells you about a new version. It does not install it.

Release notes for Voice 0.1.0 on GitHub

3 November 20262.2.0

Meetings and updates that install themselves

Live meetings in Rukoo, permission levels for chats, better booking pages, and in-place updates.

Version 2.2.0 was the largest release since 2.1.0. It added meetings, gave each assistant chat a permission level, improved booking pages again, and taught Rukoo to install its own updates.

Meetings came through a new companion app, Rukoo Voice. Voice has its own entry on this page, because it had a release of its own the same morning. Inside Rukoo, meetings live in a new third area called Meet, next to Mail and Calendar. While Voice records, Rukoo shows the written text of the call as it happens, next to your assistant.

You could start a recording from Rukoo, from a calendar appointment with "Record with Rukoo Voice", or from Voice itself. You could pause, continue, mark a moment and stop from either app. Voice told the voices apart while it recorded: Speaker 1, Speaker 2, and so on. You could give each voice a name from the guests of the calendar appointment, and the name stayed on the right voice when Voice corrected a passage or restarted. A meeting could record the screen too, either as still pictures with the text read from the screen, or as video. The pictures appeared in the written text at the moment they were taken, and your assistant could look at a picture or a stretch of the meeting.

You could ask your assistant about the meeting while it ran: "Catch me up", "What did they ask me", "Write the notes", "Draft the follow-up email". The assistant treated the meeting text and the screen text as untrusted material. In plain words, words spoken on a call or shown on a screen could not order the assistant around. The assistant also could not start or stop a recording. While a meeting recorded, Rukoo hid its own windows from screen recordings and screen sharing on Windows and Mac, and held back its own messages while the screen recorded. Settings could turn the hiding off, and could also decide whether assistants may read meetings at all.

Each assistant chat got a permission level: Ask, Auto or Full permission. Ask is the careful level Rukoo always had. The assistant asks before it acts. Full permission lets it act without the card. Settings set the normal level for new chats, and a shield next to Send showed and changed the level of the chat on screen. The risk is plain and the settings do not hide it. At Full permission an assistant can delete mail and take other lasting steps without asking.

You could also send a message while the assistant was still working. Sending normally steered the assistant. It read your new message after its current step and adjusted. A second key choice queued your message as the next request instead. A small repair rode along: an email dragged onto the chat now stayed there while the panel redrew itself. Before, a redraw at the wrong moment could quietly drop it.

Writing mail got two helps. Typing @ in the writer let you mention a person by name. Rukoo added that person as a copy recipient, so they saw they were mentioned without becoming the main reader. Right-clicking in the writer gave you spelling suggestions for a word with a red line under it, plus cut, copy and paste. Before, right-clicking there showed nothing.

Booking pages grew in four ways, and these four have public screenshots. Each booking could get its own Zoom, Teams or Jitsi video meeting link. Jitsi works without extra setup. Zoom and Teams need a small app registration of your own with those services. Guests could choose how long the meeting lasts, from lengths you offer. The invitation for a booking carried links to move or cancel it, so the guest did not have to hunt for them. The part of the meeting type editor that says when guests can book got its own clear section, and booking pages showed Rukoo's picture in the browser tab, as normal web pages do.

Updates changed the most in daily use. Instead of only opening the release page, Rukoo could now download an update and install it in place, keeping your accounts, settings, signatures and chats. You picked a channel: Stable for normal releases, or Nightly if you wanted the newest build each day and accepted rougher edges. The sidebar and Settings showed the download, then "Restart to update". If a download failed, Rukoo fell back to the release page button.

The phone, as version 0.5.0, caught up with the calmer inbox groups from 2.1.1: group labels, "Show in Inbox", and quiet groups. It also offered the same six meeting tools as the computer, so an assistant that reached you through the phone saw one steady list of tools. Those tools answered that meetings live in Rukoo on the computer.

Three small fixes closed the version. In month view, a booking request no longer hides behind "+N more" on a busy day in a long month. A long update text in the sidebar now ends with three dots instead of running off the button. Pressing Escape or Tab in a menu returns the keyboard focus to the menu's button even when the screen redrew in between, which matters if you work without a mouse.

About the screenshots for this version: meetings in Rukoo, booking pages and updates have public screenshots, shown above. The permission levels, steering a working assistant, @ mentions, the writer's spelling menu, who is speaking labels, screen recording details, meeting backup and the phone group changes belong to the private-list batch. This entry describes them from the public release notes and links the public code changes here: permission levels, steer or queue, mentions, spelling menu, speaker labels, screen recording, meeting backup and phone groups.

Release notes for 2.2.0 on GitHub

30 October 20262.1.2

Answer invitations from the mail itself

Yes, Maybe and No on the invitation mail, calendar files that open in Rukoo, and a right-click menu in mail.

Version 2.1.2 made calendar invitations in mail useful, and gave mails a right-click menu.

An invitation mail now shows a card above the mail with the title, time, video call link, place and guests, and Yes, Maybe and No buttons. If one of your calendars already holds the appointment, your answer goes through that calendar, and Google or your calendar service tells the organizer. If not, Rukoo emails the answer to the organizer from the account the invitation came to. A line under the buttons says which of the two will happen before you click, so there is no guessing. A cancelled appointment shows as cancelled. When a guest answers an appointment of yours, the card shows who answered what.

"Add to calendar" copies the appointment into a calendar you pick, with its time, place, description and repeat rule. Once it sits in your calendar, the card offers "Open in calendar" instead. The copy carries no guests, so later changes from the organizer do not reach it. The card does not hide that.

Calendar files with the ".ics" ending open in Rukoo too. That is the standard file form for a single appointment. An attached file opens as the same card in a small window, and so does a file you open with Rukoo from your file manager. On Windows, the installer puts Rukoo in "Open with" and in the default apps list for these files, without taking the default away from Outlook.

Right-clicking in a mail now gives you a menu that fits what you clicked. A link can open in your browser or copy its address. An email link can start a new mail or copy the address. A picture can open in your picture viewer, copy, or save as a file. Selected text copies, and Select all selects the whole mail. The quoted mail inside a reply has the same menu.

About the screenshots for this version: both changes belong to the batch whose screenshots sit in the private work list. There is no public screenshot to show here. The public code changes are invitations and calendar files and the right-click menu in mail. The phone did not change in this version, and it does not show invitation cards.

Release notes for 2.1.2 on GitHub

30 October 20262.1.1

Calmer inbox groups

Group labels on every mail, groups that can stay out of Inbox, and groups that can stay quiet.

Version 2.1.1 was a small release with one theme: inbox groups that are easier to live with.

Every mail now shows its group as a small colored label wherever groups mix, such as Inbox, All accounts, search results, and the VIP and Unread views. Inside a group's own view, the color sits in the list heading instead. If you have several accounts, the account became a small colored dot on the sender's picture, so it no longer looks like a second group label.

Each group got a "Show in Inbox" switch. Turn it off, and that group's mail leaves your Inbox and All accounts views. Its unread mail stops counting in the inbox count, the account menu, the taskbar badge and the tray picture. You can still find it in the group's own view, in search, and in VIP and Unread. The switch travels with your Rukoo account, so your other devices follow it.

Each group also got its own notifications switch, on by default. Mail in a quiet group sends no computer message. If Jev still has to sort a new mail, its message waits for Jev's answer, at most 20 seconds, so a quiet group's mail does not shout before it is sorted. This switch stays on the computer where you set it. Hiding a group does not quiet it, and quieting it does not hide it. For a group you want out of sight and quiet, you use both switches.

"Mark all as read" now marks what the list shows. In Inbox it leaves hidden groups alone. In a group's view it marks only that group.

Two fixes rode along. Changing the From address to an address of another account now swaps in that account's signature and booking link, in new mail, replies and reopened drafts. Calendar appointments show their calendar's color at full strength. Google's soft colors had come out almost white in the light look and grey in the dark look.

About the screenshots for this version: the color fix has public screenshots, shown above. The group label, hide and quiet changes were finished in the batch whose screenshots sit in the private work list, so this page cannot show them. You can read the public code changes here: labels, quiet groups, hidden groups and signature swap. The phone did not get "Show in Inbox" in this version. Its inbox still showed every group. That arrived on the phone in 2.2.0.

Release notes for 2.1.1 on GitHub

28 October 20262.1.0

A full calendar and booking pages

Month view, reminders, free time at a glance, and a page where people can book a time with you.

Version 2.1.0 was the first full 2.x release. It included everything from the 2.0.0 test release, now settled. On top of that, it gave the calendar the things you use a calendar for every day, and it gave your Rukoo account a booking page.

The calendar got a month view and a small month in the sidebar for jumping around. You could press G to go to a date and slash to search. You could drag across the week view to create an appointment, and drag appointments to move them or make them longer or shorter, with Undo if you dropped one in the wrong place. The appointment window grew up too. It had guests, repeating appointments with a choice of "only this one, this one and the ones after, or all of them", Google Meet links, reminders, time zone, busy or free, and who may see the appointment. You could move an appointment to another calendar or copy it. Each calendar got its own color. New calendar settings covered the first day of the week, weekends, working hours, and the normal length and reminder for new appointments.

Rukoo also started reminding you. It showed a computer message before your appointments, caught up after your computer had slept, and showed only one reminder when the same meeting sat on two calendars. Google appointments kept their own reminder times. For mail-account calendars, new appointments kept their time zone properly, so a weekly appointment no longer jumped an hour when the clocks changed.

A new panel listed your free time across every calendar that counts. You picked a length, a period and the hours of the day, and Rukoo listed the gaps that fit. If it could not read one of your accounts, it said so by name instead of pretending that time was free. While writing a mail, you could insert the same list into the message, which saves the usual back-and-forth of "does Tuesday work for you".

The booking page took that idea one step further. In Settings you could publish a page at an address with your chosen name, with your meeting types and the hours you offer. Other people opened it in a web browser, in English or Dutch, and picked a time. The page worked even with browser scripts turned off. A booking landed in the calendar you chose. A meeting type could also wait for your OK first, with Accept and Decline buttons right on the calendar. If you moved or deleted a booked appointment, the guest's page updated to match. After a booking, the guest's name, email address and note were kept locked with a key only your devices have, the same idea as the Rukoo account.

The booking page was also built for other people's assistants. Each page had a short guide that an assistant could read, a ready-made link an assistant could hand to its user, and a way for programs to ask for free times and book them. Your mail signature could end with the line "Want to meet with me? Pick a time, or share this link with your agent." Your own assistants in Rukoo got matching tools. They could list your appointments, find free time, fetch your booking link, and create an appointment after asking you first.

A "What's new" guide walked through the new inbox groups on the first start and set them up in order, and you could open it again later from Settings. The groups themselves moved from tabs above the mail list to a list under Inbox in the sidebar, which left the list more room. On the phone they sat under Inbox in the folder drawer. While Jev sorted, a line in the sidebar counted along, said why it was waiting if the service was busy, and opened a panel with Jev's recent choices when you clicked it.

You could choose what swiping left and right does to a mail, on touch screens and on the phone, and put up to four quick buttons on a mail under the mouse. Keyboard shortcuts could follow the layout of the mail app you came from: Rukoo, Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail or Thunderbird. Every six hours, Rukoo asked GitHub whether a newer release existed and showed an "Update to" button that opened the release page. It installed nothing by itself in this version. Installing updates in place arrived in 2.2.0.

The phone, as version 0.4.0, got swipe actions, groups under Inbox in the folder drawer, and the new assistant calendar tools. Those tools answered honestly that the phone had no calendar yet.

This version also carried a long list of small fixes. In plain words: account names in the account switcher now match the names in Settings. Setup explains when Gmail and Yahoo need a special app password, before sign-in fails. Unread counts include older inbox mail, not only the newest 300. Odd, deeply nested mails and a failing folder no longer stall the check for new mail. An email attached inside another email stays readable after it moves. An opened mail stays in the Unread view until you open another one, instead of vanishing under your eyes. A mail started from an email link keeps what the link filled in if you close the window. Chat replies and the chat panel behave at in-between zoom sizes. An out-of-date Hermes connecting program is reported as out of date, not as a wrong key. Mac email links and the Mac menu bar picture were fixed. Limits were added on how much a hostile mail server or sorting service could make your device download and keep.

One address changed in this version. New Rukoo accounts live at rukoo.io, and booking pages at meet.rukoo.io. A computer that made its account at the older address with 2.0.0 kept working there. To move, you deleted the account in Settings and made it again, and your booking page name stayed yours.

Release notes for 2.1.0 on GitHub

27 October 20262.0.0

An inbox that sorts itself

Inbox groups such as Needs you and Money, kept in step by a locked Rukoo account.

Version 2.0.0 was marked as a test release. It added the two ideas that later versions build on: inbox groups, and a Rukoo account that keeps those groups in step across your devices.

Turn on inbox groups in Settings, and your inbox gets tabs: Needs you, To read, Money, Updates and Promotions, next to All. The idea is close to Gmail's tabs, but it works for every mail account, not only Gmail. You could rename the groups, describe them in your own words, change their colors and order, add your own up to 12, or delete ones you do not want. Nothing moved on your mail account itself. Other mail apps kept seeing your inbox as before. Only Rukoo's view changed.

Rukoo sorted mail by looking at the sender and at the hidden labels mail carries with it, such as "this is a mailing list" or "this was sent automatically". On Gmail accounts it also used Gmail's own tabs. If it put a mail in the wrong group, you picked "Move to category" to correct it. "Also future mail" applied the same choice to that sender from then on. Mail that Rukoo could not place with confidence went to a group you chose for that case.

If you wanted help with the doubtful cases, you could add your own key for a sorting service called Jev, made by a company called TypeSafe. This was off until you added a key. With it on, Rukoo sent Jev the sender, the subject and the first 1,000 characters of each doubtful mail, plus your group names and descriptions, and Jev picked a group. The release notes said plainly where that text went, so you could decide with open eyes.

The Rukoo account kept your groups, the group each mail got, and your corrections the same on all your devices. You made it in Settings with your email address, a password and an invite code. Rukoo locked the data on your device with a key that only your devices have, before anything left the device. Your password never left the device at all. You got a recovery key once, for the day you forget your password. The account page listed your devices so you could sign one out, and it offered the normal account actions: change password, new recovery key, download your data, sign out, delete account. Without an account, groups still worked on one device.

A page called "What's stored and shared" spelled out what the account computer could and could not see. It could see your email address, your device names, when they checked in, and how many locked records you had and how large they were. It could not see your mail, your groups, or what was in them, because it never got the key. At this point the account computer lived at an address run by the maintainer, with the data stored in the European Union. Anyone who copies Rukoo could run their own account computer instead. The phone got the same account and groups in this version, and kept them in step with the computer.

Two warnings belong here, because they still apply. New accounts needed an invite code, until the account computer could check email addresses properly. And if you forget both your password and your recovery key, the account data is gone for good. Nobody can open it for you, because nobody else has the key. That is the price of the lock, and the settings say so before you start.

Release notes for 2.0.0 on GitHub

26 October 20261.6.0

Small phone fixes you feel every day

Editable chat shortcuts on Android, and Previous and Next move to the bottom bar.

Version 1.6.0 changed nothing on the computer. It polished the phone, and it put Rukoo under the MIT license. That is a short, permissive open-source license. In short, other people may use, copy and build on the code, as long as they keep the license note.

On the phone, the chat shortcuts became editable, just as on the computer. The round button after the shortcuts in a new chat used to open Settings without a way to edit anything. Now it opened the shortcut page. You could move shortcuts up and down, take one out of new chats, rename one or rewrite its instructions, and add your own. The phone kept its own list.

Reading mail got easier on the thumb. Previous and Next moved from a menu at the top of the screen to the bottom bar, at the bottom right, next to the assistant button. They grey out at the first and last mail. When the bar runs out of room, Reply shows only its picture and a long assistant name gets shortened, so nothing falls off the edge.

Release notes for 1.6.0 on GitHub

23 October 20261.5.0

Rukoo on your phone

Rukoo for Android, built for the Galaxy Z Fold7, with assistants on the phone and through your computer.

Version 1.5.0 added Rukoo for Android. It was marked as a test version. It was built first for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold7, the phone that folds open into a small tablet, and it needed Android 12 or newer.

On the phone you got your mail: Gmail with Google sign-in, other mail accounts, and the sample account. You got folders, combined views across accounts, search, swipe actions with Undo, a proper reader for formatted mail, and a writer with formatting. Drafts saved to the Drafts folder of your mail account, so a draft started on the phone was there on the computer. New mail could notify you.

The assistant chat came with it. It had the same quick actions, skills, model choices, plans and approval cards as the computer version. An assistant could write a draft straight into the phone's writer for you to check. A chat message could carry files, photos and the email on your screen. On the Fold7, the small outer screen showed one thing at a time and the large inner screen showed two columns. Folding or unfolding the phone kept your open email, chat and draft where they were.

How the assistants reached the phone split in two. Hermes assistants, including the maintainer's own assistant Clark, and OpenClaw could talk to the phone directly over Tailscale. Claude Code and Codex run on a computer, not on a phone. For them, the phone could borrow your computer. You paired the phone with Rukoo on the computer using an address and a short code, and you could send your accounts and assistant settings over once during pairing. After that, a Claude Code or Codex chat started on the phone ran on the computer, while its mail tools acted on the phone's mail and writer. The computer had to be on, with Rukoo open and Tailscale running. Rukoo only accepted the phone on its Tailscale address, and only while you left the pairing switch on.

Clark learned the same trick from the other side. The phone offered Rukoo's mail tools on its Tailscale address, and the small connecting program on the Hermes computer learned to look for phones as well as computers. A chat with Clark started on the phone could then read the phone's mail and write into the phone's writer.

Three smaller phone records show the level of finish. Folders got a sheet that slides up on the small screen, so they are always in reach. The writer got bold, italic and underline through the normal text selection menu. Files and photos could be attached to a chat, with a clear message when an assistant could not read a file.

The phone limits were stated plainly, and most of them still apply at the end of this story. The phone had no calendar yet. Mail did not arrive the instant it was sent. The phone checked every few minutes while open and every 15 minutes in the background. The phone writer had no text colors, highlights, indenting or pictures inside the text, so a computer draft that used them lost that styling if you opened and saved it on the phone. The words stayed. Google sign-in on the phone itself, OpenClaw on the phone, and Clark using the phone's tools from a phone chat had not yet been tried on a real phone.

Release notes for 1.5.0 on GitHub

21 October 20261.4.0

Proper signatures and a fourth assistant

Formatted signatures with pictures, and OpenClaw joins Hermes, Claude Code and Codex.

Version 1.4.0 fixed signatures, and it added a fourth kind of assistant.

Before this version, a signature was plain text. Now you could paste a formatted signature from Outlook, Gmail or a web page, or build one in Settings with bold text, colors, links, tables and pictures. People who know web code could edit that code directly. It worked as one general signature, or a different one per account, and it appeared in new mail, replies, forwards and drafts, in both the built-in write area and the separate write window. Rukoo stripped out anything that could run code, and the plain-text copy of your mail got a readable version of the same signature. An old plain-text signature kept working as before.

Pictures in mail were fixed at the same time. Pictures you put in a mail, including pictures in a signature, now traveled in the form that Gmail and Outlook actually show. Before, a mail could look right in Rukoo and arrive without its pictures at the other end.

The fourth assistant is OpenClaw. It joined Hermes, Claude Code and Codex in Settings. You connected it with the address of your OpenClaw computer and its key, and Rukoo showed whether the connection worked. Replies appeared word by word in the chat, each chat kept its own conversation, and the Stop button stopped the work at the other end too. A "Copy OpenClaw setup" button gave you the one command that lets OpenClaw use Rukoo's mail and calendar tools. That worked when OpenClaw ran on the same computer, and also when it ran on another computer in your private Tailscale network, such as a small home server, once you turned on the switch that allows it. Tailscale is a service that links your own devices as if they were on one home network, even when they are far apart.

The release notes were open about one limit. OpenClaw in Rukoo had only been tested against a pretend OpenClaw, not yet against a real one over a real network. The chat also showed only OpenClaw's words, not the steps it took to get there.

Release notes for 1.4.0 on GitHub

19 October 20261.3.0

Mac and Linux, and chats that call you back

Rukoo arrives on Mac and Linux, and the chat panel shows which chats have a reply ready.

Rukoo started as a Windows app. Version 1.3.0 brought it to Mac and Linux computers as well.

On a Mac, Rukoo came as a normal Mac download for both newer and older Macs. It used Mac menus and Mac keyboard shortcuts, showed the unread count on its picture in the Dock, and could open email links. Passwords and assistant keys went into the Mac's own Keychain, where Mac apps keep secrets. On Linux, Rukoo came in two common Linux forms, with a normal app launcher and the same email link choice. Passwords went into the Linux key stores. On both systems, Rukoo could find assistants you had installed in the usual places.

The chat panel also learned to keep track of chats you had left alone. A chat kept working when you opened another email. A bell at the top of the panel counted the chats with a reply you had not seen, or with a question waiting for your approval. Orange meant an assistant was waiting for you. Blue meant a reply was ready. The bell's list showed each chat and what it was doing: working, waiting for you, reply ready, stopped with an error, or simply the start of the last message. Picking a chat opened it together with its email, even if that email had moved to another folder in the meantime. With the panel closed, a small dot on the chat button told you something was waiting. Rukoo remembered which replies you had not read after a restart.

Two practical notes came with the new systems. Mac downloads were only fully approved by Apple when the release was built with Apple developer papers, so some downloads needed an extra OK from the system. On Linux, Rukoo needed your key store unlocked to save account passwords. Without one, the sample account still worked, but real accounts could not be saved.

Release notes for 1.3.0 on GitHub

16 October 20261.2.0

Your own shortcuts and faster mail

Arrange the chat shortcuts, start assistant skills with the dollar sign, and open mail faster.

Version 1.2.0 made the assistant chat yours to arrange, and it made mail open faster.

A new chat offers shortcut buttons such as "Draft a reply" and "Brief me". In this version you could arrange them in Settings. You could move them up or down, hide one from new chats, give one a new name, or change the instructions it sends to the assistant. You could also add your own, with its own name, picture and instructions. A hidden shortcut still worked if you typed its command. Rukoo kept up to 40 shortcuts, and they worked the same with every assistant.

Your assistants have skills of their own, on top of the ones Rukoo brings. Think of a skill as a practiced routine, such as preparing for a meeting in a set way. In 1.2.0 you could type the dollar sign in the chat box to see the skills of the assistant in that chat, pick one, and send it with your message. The skill appeared in your message as a small label with its name, so you could see what you had asked for. Rukoo's own skills kept their slash commands, such as typing a name after a slash to start one.

Mail itself got quicker in three ways. A long email with pictures used to stay squashed into a thin strip until the last picture on the internet had loaded. Now it showed at full height right away. After each check for new mail, Rukoo quietly downloaded your newest 30 inbox messages in the background, without marking them as read, so opening them felt instant. A message that was not downloaded yet fetched itself on its own line, instead of waiting behind a check for new mail. Checks also asked the mail service only for what could have changed, so they finished much sooner.

Last, Rukoo could open email links from other apps. If you clicked an email address in your web browser, Windows could open a Rukoo write window with the address, subject and text already filled in.

Release notes for 1.2.0 on GitHub

14 October 20261.1.0

Calendars for other mail accounts

Mail accounts other than Google show their calendars in the same view.

In this version, mail accounts other than Google got their calendars too.

Many mail accounts come with a calendar service of their own. The technical name for that service is CalDAV, and you will see that word in the settings. In plain words, it is the address where your mail provider keeps your appointments. In 1.1.0 you could type that address in the account settings, and Rukoo would check it before saving. Your appointments then appeared in the same calendar view as your Google ones, in the color of that account.

Weekly and monthly appointments showed every time they happened, including a single time that you had moved or skipped in another app. You could add, change and delete appointments, or change just one time in a series. If your calendar service told the organizer for you, you could also answer invitations with Yes, Maybe or No. If the service refused your password, the calendar said so in normal words and gave you a button that took you straight to the right settings page.

This version also fixed a small Windows mix-up. If you ran Rukoo from its source code as a developer, the installed app could end up with the wrong picture in the taskbar. After the fix, the two kept their own pictures.

Some care is still built in here. Appointments with guests, rooms or equipment on them cannot be changed from Rukoo when they live on this kind of calendar service, because the service might email the guests or change a room booking without asking you first. You can still read them and, where the service allows it, answer them. Ready-made settings for iCloud and Fastmail were not in yet, and Microsoft sign-in was still missing.

Release notes for 1.1.0 on GitHub

13 October 20261.0.0

The first release

Mail, calendar and assistant chat in one Windows app, with a sample account to try it all.

The first version already had the three parts that define Rukoo: mail, calendar and assistant chat.

For mail, you could connect Gmail and Google Workspace accounts with "Sign in with Google". You could also connect Yahoo, Outlook, work mail and other accounts in the usual mail app way. All your accounts could share one inbox. You could search, use quick filters such as unread mail, and undo a delete, an archive or a move if you acted too fast. Drafts saved to your mail account while you wrote, so a half-written mail was still there if you closed the app. New mail could show a Windows message, and the button in the taskbar showed how much unread mail you had.

For the calendar, Rukoo showed the calendars of all your Google accounts together. You could look at a week, a day, or a list of what is coming up. You could add, change and delete appointments and answer invitations. If someone changed the same appointment in Google Calendar while you had it open, Rukoo did not quietly overwrite their change. It kept the version question visible instead.

For assistant chat, you could connect your own Hermes assistant, Claude Code or Codex. These are AI assistants that run on your own computer or on a computer you control. In Rukoo they could read mail and write draft replies for you to check. They could not send mail themselves, and they had to ask before doing anything that other people would see. You could add files and other emails to a chat, so the assistant had the full picture. Two ready-made requests came with the app: one to unsubscribe from a sender, and one to ask a sender to delete your data. You could pick which AI model a chat used and how hard it should think.

Rukoo kept running near the clock when you closed the window, so it could tell you about new mail without sitting open on your screen. It worked in English and Dutch, in a light and a dark look, and you could make everything larger or smaller, from 80% to 200%. A sample account with made-up mail and appointments let you try everything without connecting a real account first.

Two limits mattered on day one, and both got work in later versions. Signing in with Google needed a small Google project of your own, because Rukoo did not bring one with it. Most Outlook.com and Microsoft 365 mailboxes needed a Microsoft sign-in that Rukoo did not have yet, and the calendar only worked for Google accounts. Each mail folder kept only its newest messages on your computer: 300 for the inbox and 100 for other folders. Older mail stayed on your mail account.

Release notes for 1.0.0 on GitHub

Good to know

The downloads are not signed yet. On Windows, the system warns before the first start of Rukoo and of Rukoo Voice. You choose "More info", then "Run anyway". On Linux, Rukoo needs your key store unlocked to save passwords.

The phone has no calendar yet, and mail on the phone does not arrive the instant it is sent. It checks every few minutes while open and every 15 minutes in the background. A mail with a large attachment still downloads in full before you can read its text.

Two keys deserve a safe place outside your computer: the Rukoo account recovery key and the Rukoo Voice recovery code. If you lose your password and the recovery help together, nobody can open that data again, because the key never leaves your devices.

One batch of screenshots is missing from this page. For a group of changes finished on 29 and 30 October 2026, the screenshots sit in a private work list instead of on GitHub. Those entries describe the change and link the public code, and say so where it happens.
